Baby & Child

24-hour urine collection for children: a practical guide

Updated: November 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Collecting urine for a whole day and night takes planning, especially when a child is uncomfortable or needs help using the toilet. The aim is a complete, correctly timed sample. Get the laboratory’s written instructions before starting: the bottle, preservative and storage requirements depend on the test ordered.

What this collection measures

A clinician may need the total amount of urine, or the amount of a particular substance passed during a day. A timed collection lets the laboratory assess that period rather than a single visit to the toilet. Ask what is being measured and who will explain the result; the request alone does not diagnose kidney disease.

This is different from a small clean-catch or midstream sample. Instructions to discard the first few drops of every sample do not apply to a standard 24-hour collection. After the starting bladder emptying is discarded, all urine passed during the collection period is needed, including overnight urine.

Arrange the equipment and a workable day

Obtain the laboratory’s storage bottle, label, request form and carrying bag. Ask for a suitable collection device, such as a toilet collection hat, plastic urinal or approved clean, dry, non-metal jug, and a funnel if needed. Use the supplied storage container; if it may fill up, arrange another approved bottle rather than improvising with a drinks bottle.

A day at home may be easiest. If your child must go out, plan how every toilet visit and the required storage will be managed. Explain the steps simply and tell anyone sharing their care. Ask the team before starting if your child uses nappies, has frequent accidents or has a catheter: they need an appropriate collection plan, not an improvised adaptation of toilet-trained instructions.

Check food, medicines and preservative precautions

Ask whether this particular test needs changes to food or drink. Otherwise follow the child’s usual or prescribed intake; do not force extra water to produce a bigger sample. Tell the team about medicines and supplements, and do not stop prescribed treatment yourself. Ask about menstruation or other circumstances that may affect the sample.

Liquid already in the bottle may be a necessary preservative, sometimes a corrosive acid. Do not pour it out, rinse the storage bottle or add a homemade preservative. Keep it out of children’s reach and let an adult transfer urine carefully from the separate collection device. Never have the child urinate directly into a preservative bottle. If preservative splashes onto skin or into eyes, immediately rinse with plenty of running water and obtain urgent medical advice.

Start by discarding one bladder emptying

Choose the start time with the laboratory’s instructions in mind; morning is often convenient. At that time, ask the child to empty their bladder into the toilet and discard that urine. Write down the actual date and time straight away. The collection begins after this emptying; any preservative must remain in the storage bottle.

For example, if the starting urine is passed at 8 a.m. on Monday, the intended finish is 8 a.m. on Tuesday. Keep this target visible and plan for the next morning. Do not save the starting urine simply because it is the first urine of the day: doing so would include urine made before the timed period.

Collect every subsequent urination, including overnight

For each toilet visit, catch all the urine in the approved device and transfer it to the storage bottle. Follow the laboratory’s instructions for cleaning or replacing the collection device between uses. Keep toilet paper, stool and other material out of the sample; when the child needs a bowel movement, arrange to catch the urine separately.

Replace the cap securely after each transfer and return the bottle to its required storage place. A reminder by the toilet and an agreed handover between carers can help prevent a missed visit. Give the child privacy and calm assistance. If collecting is becoming distressing or impractical, contact the team for help rather than blaming the child or disguising an incomplete sample.

Include the final urine at the planned finish

At the end of the 24 hours, ask the child to try to empty their bladder into the collection device and add this final urine to the bottle. This final emptying is included, unlike the one at the start. Record the actual finishing date and time, including whether it is morning or evening.

If the child cannot pass urine near the planned time, or the schedule goes wrong, ask the laboratory what to do and record what actually happened. Do not force fluids, make the child hold urine for longer, or enter a time that was not observed. The laboratory needs an honest account to judge whether the collection can be used.

Storage rules belong to the ordered test

Many children’s laboratories require the bottle to stay refrigerated, or in an appropriately iced cooler, throughout collection and transport. Other protocols permit cool, light-protected storage for particular samples. Confirm the requirement for your bottle before starting and follow it throughout; a general article cannot decide which rule fits the requested analysis.

Do not assume that any urine sample can wait at room temperature for one or two days. Keep the bottle tightly closed, protected from heat and stored safely as instructed. Do not freeze it unless the laboratory specifically directs you to. If it was left too warm or otherwise stored incorrectly, report the timing and conditions rather than assuming later refrigeration fixes the problem.

Report missed urine, spills or contamination

Tell the laboratory if any urine was missed, spilled or mixed with stool, or if preservative was lost. Describe when it happened and roughly how much urine was missed if you know. An incomplete collection may underestimate the amount passed and affect interpretation. Depending on the test and the problem, the laboratory may ask you to start again.

Do not top up the bottle with water or extend the collection to make up a missed toilet visit. Ask whether you need a new bottle and preservative before restarting; a cleaning instruction for an empty non-preservative bottle may be unsafe for a different container. Reporting a mistake is useful information, not a failure by you or your child.

Label, return and arrange the result

Check the child’s full name, date of birth or other required identifier, requesting clinician or clinic, and exact start and finish dates and times. Label every bottle if more than one was used. Secure the lids, use the supplied carrying bag and take the request form. Return the complete collection promptly using the laboratory’s transport and temperature instructions.

Check opening hours before your collection day and ask what to do if delivery will be delayed. Confirm how and when the clinician will discuss the results; turnaround depends on the tests. A scheduled collection should not delay care if your child becomes unwell. Tell their care team about illness or difficulties that arise during the collection.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Read the laboratory’s instructions together before starting, especially its preservative and temperature requirements.

Write down the actual start and finish times and any collection problems for the laboratory.

Ask for individual help with nappies, continence difficulties, distress or an existing catheter.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organize the collection schedule, questions and result appointment. It cannot certify a sample as complete, choose its storage conditions or interpret a laboratory result.

When to seek help

Preservatives may be corrosive: keep them out of children’s reach, avoid direct contact and rinse splashes immediately with running water while obtaining urgent medical advice. Do not change prescribed medicines or fluid restrictions yourself. A urine collection must not delay care for an unwell child.

Evidence notes updated: November 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Confirm the correct bottle, preparation, storage and delivery instructions before starting.
  • Discard the starting bladder emptying, then collect all urine and include the final emptying at 24 hours.
  • Preservative stays in the bottle; protect the child from contact or splashes.
  • Record actual times and report missed urine or contamination honestly.
  • Use the laboratory’s advice for restarting and for children who need extra collection support.

Frequently asked questions

What equipment do we need?

Ask the laboratory for the correct storage bottle, label, request form and bag, plus a suitable collection hat, urinal or other approved device. A funnel may help transfer urine. Check whether a second bottle or a way to maintain the required temperature will be needed.

Why collect urine for a whole day?

The clinician may need the total urine volume or the amount of a substance passed over that period. All urine during the timed interval is needed. A small spot sample answers a different question and cannot simply replace the ordered collection.

Should I empty the liquid already in the bottle?

No. It may be an essential preservative and can be corrosive. Leave it in place, keep the bottle away from children and avoid splashes. If it has been emptied or spilled, contact the laboratory before proceeding.

What if my child cannot use the funnel?

Use a laboratory-approved collection device, such as a toilet hat, plastic urinal or clean, dry, non-metal jug, then transfer the urine carefully. A household plant pot is not suitable. Keep urine separate from stool and ask for help if the method is not working.

Does the first morning urine go into the bottle?

Discard the bladder emptying that starts the collection and record its time. Include all subsequent urine, including the final emptying near the same time the next day. The distinction is the start and finish of the timed period, not simply whether it is morning.

Does the bottle have to stay in the fridge?

Often yes, including during collection, but requirements depend on the test and preservative. Follow the instructions from the laboratory supplying your bottle. Ask before starting if storage or transport arrangements are unclear.

Do we have to restart after one missed visit?

Report it to the laboratory. Some protocols require a new collection, while the team may assess the effect in other circumstances. Do not silently submit it as complete or reuse a preservative bottle without instructions.

Can I use a nappy sample for the whole-day collection?

Do not squeeze urine from a nappy or substitute a spot-sample technique for a timed collection. Contact the child’s nurse or laboratory before starting so they can arrange an appropriate method and explain what to do about leaks or missed urine.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
